title: How to Choose the Right Short Track Speed Skating Blade
thumbnail_text: Pick the right short track blade first time

scenes.heading: How to Choose a Short Track Blade
scenes.sub: Flex, length, steel, bend and cups, explained so you buy once
scenes.chapter: Choosing a blade: the short answer
scenes.narration: This video shows you how to choose a short track speed skating blade that suits you, so you can buy once and buy well. We will cover flex, length, steel, bend, cups and mounting, one at a time. Your blades are the only contact point between you and the ice. They decide how you carry speed, how you hold a line through a corner, and how confident you feel when you commit to an apex. A blade that suits your style feels like part of your body. A blade that does not will fight you on every lap.

scenes.heading: Why the blade matters most
bullets: The blade is where power becomes motion
It turns your push into forward speed
It holds a stable edge in the corner
It releases smoothly into the next stride
scenes.narration: Boots, bearings and suits all play a part. But the blade is where your power becomes motion. A good blade turns your push cleanly into forward speed. It keeps a stable edge when you load it in the corner. And it releases smoothly as you move from one stride to the next. Short track is raced on tight corners at high speed. So small differences in flex, bend and steel quality make large differences in how the skate behaves under pressure.

scenes.heading: Understanding flex
bullets: Flex is how much the blade bends
More flex feels forgiving and flowing
Stiffer returns energy more directly
Lighter, technical skaters often like flex
Heavier, powerful skaters often want firm
scenes.narration: Flex is how much the blade bends along its length when you load it. Most skaters notice it first. A more flexible blade moves with your push. It absorbs small mistakes in technique and feels forgiving. It lets the skate flow through a corner with a natural rhythm. A stiffer blade returns energy more directly. It feels sharp, holds a very firm line, and responds the moment you drive hard. Neither one is better in absolute terms. The right flex depends on your weight, your power, and how you like a corner to feel. As a general rule, lighter and more technical skaters enjoy more flex. Heavier and more powerful skaters tend to want a firmer platform.

scenes.heading: The flex spectrum
scenes.narration: Here is the range on a single flex scale. On the left, in green, is the soft end: more flex and more feel. On the right, in orange, is the firm end: more hold and a more direct response. The JaeBee sits at the soft end. Its tube tapers toward the ends, so the tips give more and the flex builds progressively. In the middle is a blade with even stiffness along its full length, a stable platform for skaters who want a little more hold. At the firm end is the XC Flex Weapon, built for maximum corner hold while still gliding well. Pick your spot on this line by feel, flow or hold.

scenes.heading: Blade length
bullets: Match length to boot, height and style
Shorter blades change direction quickly
Longer blades track straighter
Find your window, then fine tune
scenes.narration: Next is length. You choose it to match your boot size, your height and your racing style. Shorter blades change direction quickly and feel lively. That suits tight, reactive skating. Longer blades track straighter and carry more speed on the straights. That suits smooth, powerful skaters who like stability. Most skaters settle within a narrow window that fits their boot, and then fine tune from there. Do not guess your length. If you are unsure, send your boot size to the shop and ask which length fits.

scenes.heading: Steel: bimetal or full PM
bullets: The runner is the part on the ice
Bimetal, about 62 HRC: balance and value
Full PM, about 64 HRC: edge lasts longer
High volume training favours full PM
scenes.narration: The runner is the part that touches the ice. Its steel decides how long your edge lasts and how it feels. Bimetal runners are around 62 on the hardness scale. They give an excellent balance of performance, durability and value, and they are a smart choice for most skaters. Full PM steel is around 64, so it is harder. It holds a sharp edge longer between sharpenings. If you train a lot and hate losing your edge in the middle of a session, the harder steel pays for itself. You sharpen less often, and the feel stays more consistent.

scenes.heading: Bend and cups
bullets: Blades are bent to a corner radius
An accurate bend gives a repeatable arc
Cups join the blade to the boot
Cup height sets how far you can lean
scenes.narration: Short track blades are bent to a radius so the skate can carve a tight corner. The accuracy and smoothness of that bend matter a lot. A precise bend gives a predictable arc that repeats every time you load the blade. That builds confidence when you lean at full commitment. Cups connect the blade to your boot. Light, strong aluminium cups add stiffness and save weight. They come in different heights, so you can tune how far you lean before the boot touches the ice. A clean, straight mount is essential. If the blade is even slightly off, your edges feel unpredictable. Take your time with alignment, or ask an experienced skater to help.

scenes.heading: Anatomy of a short track blade
scenes.narration: This side view shows how the parts fit together. At the top is the boot sole. Two cups drop down from it. They are the aluminium blocks that hold the blade and set its height. Below the cups is the tube, shown in blue, with the lips in green where the tube meets the cups. At the bottom is the steel runner, bent to a corner radius. Every part in this chain affects how the edge behaves. So when something feels wrong on the ice, check each part from the boot down.

scenes.heading: Will the blades fit your boots?
scenes.narration: This is the question skaters forget to ask until the parcel is open. A blade is not a universal part. Short track boots use 165 millimetre spacing between the two mounting holes. Inline speed boots are commonly drilled at 195. If those do not match, the parts will not line up. An adapter set bridges 195 down to 165 using the existing holes, with no drilling. So measure between the centres of your two holes before you order. The lower line is cup height. Lower sits you closer to the ice and feels more stable. Higher gives a deeper lean before the boot touches. If you change height, go one millimetre at a time, and give it a few sessions before you judge it.

scenes.heading: Match the blade to your level
bullets: Newer: forgiving flex, length that fits
Intermediate: choose flex by feel
Elite: tune steel and cup height to event
Dry blades and check mounts every session
scenes.chapter: Matching a blade to your level
scenes.narration: If you are newer to short track, choose a forgiving, flexible blade and a length that fits your boot. A friendly platform helps you build good technique. Intermediate skaters can start choosing flex by the feel they prefer. Lean flexible for flow, or firmer for hold. Elite racers usually know what they want, and pick steel and cup height to match their setup and event. Whatever you choose, care for it. Sharpen consistently with a proper jig that clamps the blades straight. Wear cut resistant gloves when you work on blades. Dry your blades after every session, and check your mounts.

scenes.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Copying a champion's blade
Guessing length instead of matching boot
Ignoring steel, then losing your edge
Skipping maintenance
scenes.narration: A few mistakes come up again and again. Skaters chase the blade a champion uses, rather than the blade that suits them. They pick a length by guesswork instead of matching it to their boot. They ignore steel quality, and then wonder why their edge fades. And they skip maintenance, which quietly wears down performance. Avoid these four, and you will get far more out of whatever blade you choose. One more tip. Blades and cups can move to a new pair of boots later. Just check the mounting spacing on the new boots first.

scenes.heading: Choose by feel: flow or hold
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: So here is the short version. Choose flex by feel, flow or hold. Match the length to your boot. Pick steel by how much you train. Check your mounting spacing before you order, and change cup height one step at a time. The full guide is on the LiveLica blog, with more answers on length, cups and moving blades between boots. The link is in the description.
